title: Compare and Contrast Networking Appliances, Applications, and Functions

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Networks use specialized appliances, applications, and functions to move traffic, protect systems, distribute workloads, control wireless access, provide storage, and improve performance. CompTIA expects recognition of both physical and virtual appliances.
bullets: Router, switch, firewall, IDS, and IPS
sections.callout: Function matters more than the box: identify what the component does.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given a networking requirement, can you select the appliance, application, or function designed to solve it?
bullets: Detect → IDS; detect and prevent → IPS
Provide Wi-Fi → AP; manage APs → Controller

sections.title: Physical and Virtual Appliances
paragraphs: A network appliance can be dedicated hardware or a virtualized software appliance. Routers, firewalls, load balancers, and other functions may use either form while performing the same core role.
sections.callout: Do not identify an appliance only by its physical appearance; identify its network function.

entries.title: Router
paragraphs: A router connects different IP networks and forwards packets according to network-layer addressing.
entries.recognitionCue: Traffic must move between subnets → Router.

entries.title: Switch
paragraphs: A switch connects devices within a LAN and traditionally forwards Ethernet frames according to MAC addresses.
entries.memoryHook: Device to device on the LAN.
entries.recognitionCue: Multiple wired devices need local connectivity → Switch.

entries.title: Firewall
paragraphs: A firewall permits or blocks traffic according to security rules.
entries.recognitionCue: Enforce an allow/deny network policy → Firewall.

entries.title: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
paragraphs: An IDS monitors for suspicious activity and generates alerts without automatically stopping the traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Notify analysts of suspicious traffic → IDS.

entries.title: Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
paragraphs: An IPS detects suspicious activity and can actively block or prevent it.

entries.title: Load Balancer
paragraphs: A load balancer distributes requests across multiple systems to improve performance and availability.
entries.memoryHook: Do not make one server do everything.
entries.recognitionCue: Spread web requests among several servers → Load balancer.

entries.title: Proxy
paragraphs: A proxy acts as an intermediary between a client and another destination. It can provide filtering, access control, privacy, caching, or policy enforcement.
entries.recognitionCue: Clients access resources through an intermediary → Proxy.

entries.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
paragraphs: A CDN caches or distributes content across geographically distributed systems so users can receive it from nearby infrastructure.
entries.recognitionCue: Global users need lower-latency content delivery → CDN.

entries.title: Network-Attached Storage (NAS)
paragraphs: NAS provides file-level storage over a network through shared files and folders.
entries.recognitionCue: Users need a shared folder → NAS.

entries.title: Storage Area Network (SAN)
paragraphs: A SAN provides networked block-level storage, commonly to servers. The storage can appear like locally attached disks to the host.
entries.recognitionCue: Servers need high-speed block storage → SAN.

entries.title: Access Point (AP)
paragraphs: An AP provides wireless clients with access to the network.
entries.recognitionCue: Laptops and phones need wireless LAN access → AP.

entries.title: Wireless Controller
paragraphs: A wireless controller centrally configures and manages multiple access points.
entries.recognitionCue: Dozens of APs need centralized management → Wireless controller.

entries.title: Virtual Private Network (VPN)
paragraphs: A VPN creates a protected connection across another network for remote access or site-to-site communication.
entries.recognitionCue: A remote employee needs protected access to an internal network → VPN.

entries.title: Quality of Service (QoS)
paragraphs: QoS classifies and prioritizes traffic so time-sensitive services such as voice receive appropriate treatment when resources compete. QoS does not create additional bandwidth.
entries.recognitionCue: Voice is choppy during bulk transfers → Configure QoS.

entries.title: Time to Live (TTL)
paragraphs: Routers decrement an IP packet's TTL at each hop. When it reaches zero, the packet is discarded, preventing indefinite circulation during a routing loop.
entries.recognitionCue: Limit how long an IP packet can traverse routers → TTL.

entries.title: IDS vs. IPS
paragraphs: IDS detects and alerts. IPS detects and prevents.

entries.title: NAS vs. SAN
paragraphs: NAS presents files. SAN presents block storage.

entries.title: AP vs. Controller
paragraphs: An AP connects wireless clients. A controller manages multiple APs.

entries.title: Firewall vs. IDS/IPS
paragraphs: A firewall enforces configured traffic rules. IDS and IPS focus on detecting suspicious activity; IPS can block it.

entries.title: QoS vs. Bandwidth
paragraphs: QoS prioritizes existing capacity; it does not create more capacity.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Distribute → Load balancer or CDN, based on scenario
